kakekotoba.reading_primary: しのぶ (to endure, to conceal one's feelings)
kakekotoba.reading_secondary: しのぶ (echoes 篠 shino- of 篠原, and also evokes しのぶ草/しのぶずり, the fern/plant associated with longing)
kakekotoba.interaction: The verb しのぶれど 'though I conceal/endure it' is phonetically anchored by the preceding 篠原 (shinohara, bamboo-grass field), whose first syllables しの- prefigure しのぶ. This is not a full double-meaning pivot in the strict sense but a jokotoba-pivot: the sound しの links the physical landscape image to the psychological verb, so 忍ぶ itself functions as the hinge-word where the preface's sound resolves into the poem's real subject, concealment of love.

jokotoba.function: Describes a sparse, overgrown moor of cogon-grass and low bamboo-grass (shinohara); this landscape image is not literally relevant to the speaker's feelings but is composed specifically to phonetically generate しの, which pivots into 忍ぶ (to conceal/endure one's love), following the established jokotoba technique of using a place-image purely for its sound-bridge into the emotional statement that follows.

honkadori.source_poem: Man'yōshū-derived / associated with a poem structurally similar to 'Asajiu no ono no shinohara shinoburu ni' type utamakura poems using 浅茅生 and 篠原 as jokotoba for 忍ぶ
honkadori.function: Draws on a conventional jokotoba pattern using overgrown moor imagery (asajiu, shinohara) to introduce しのぶ, a technique inherited from earlier waka rather than a single identifiable source poem with full confidence

kigo.note: 浅茅 (asaji, cogon/cogon-grass) growing sparse and low over a moor is a classical image of desolation, most strongly associated with autumn in waka — withered or thinning grasses signal the fading of the year and by extension the fading or hidden nature of the speaker's feelings. Together with 篠原 (a field of small bamboo-grass), it evokes a bleak, untended landscape conventionally linked to autumn desolation and unfulfilled longing, reinforcing the poem's theme of concealed love breaking into open yearning.

bipartite.kami_theme: A desolate moor overgrown with sparse cogon-grass and low bamboo-grass, used as a preface whose sound generates the verb 'to endure/conceal' (shinoburedo) — the speaker states that they have been concealing their love
bipartite.shimo_theme: Despite all effort to hide and endure the feeling, it overflows uncontrollably — the speaker asks rhetorically why longing for this person has become so unbearably strong
bipartite.pivot_note: The bleak autumnal landscape of kami-no-ku is not merely decorative: it is constructed entirely to yield, through the sound しの, the verb 忍ぶ that opens shimo-no-ku. The physical image of grasses barely containing themselves on a wild moor mirrors the emotional image of a heart that can no longer contain its longing — the landscape's overgrown, uncontained quality silently prefigures the shimo's 'amarite' (overflowing), even though the connection is sonic/associative rather than a stated simile.
